"As you ask me today, I believe it's a 10 -- that we will be gone by 2011," Odierno responded. One of the key architects of the troop "surge" strategy in Iraq, Odierno said conditions in the war-torn country have "improved significantly" in the past year or so. "Obviously, we still have some very serious incidents ... but, again, it's much safer," he said. Nine U.S. troops were killed in March, the lowest monthly toll since the beginning of the Iraq War in 2003, he said.  Watch Odierno share his assessment with CNN's John King » . "So, there's been a clear improvement of security here," Odierno said. "The issue is: Can we maintain that? Can the Iraqis maintain it? And that's what we're working through now. We want them to be able to maintain this stability as we pull out." But less than two weeks into April, the U.S. toll for the month is already at nine. Asked whether the attacks were a sign of increased coordinated violence, Odierno responded that "there are some cells out there who are still capable of conducting suicide attacks," though he described the cells as "very small."  Watch as general discusses joining Facebook » . The U.S. military has made it more difficult for foreign fighters to get into Iraq through Syria, but there is still support for the Iraqi insurgency coming from Iran, he said. Mowaffak al-Rubaie, Iraqi national security adviser, said the Iraqi government is making improvements in handling its own security. "We, the government of Iraq and the security forces in Iraq are much more suited now for this fight," al-Rubaie told "State of the Union." "And we believe that now we are leading and we are planning and carrying out most of the combat operations in the country, " he said, "and the United States forces are moving or transitioning to a more support role, more training, more providing more logistical support, rather than engaging in a huge military or kinetic combat operations." Al-Rubaie was mum when asked how President Obama has differed from former President George W. Bush.  Watch al-Rubaie discuss Iraq's future » . "I don't want to elaborate on differences," al-Rubaie said. "But I believe that President Obama understands the situation in Iraq and I believe he wants to stick by ... the withdrawal agreement." Odierno described Obama as "very attentive." "He listens. He's incredibly intelligent. He talks through the issues," Odierno said. "He makes a decision and then we execute those decisions, and that's all you can expect out of your commander-in-chief. And I've been very pleased with the interaction that I've been able to have with him."

outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — Gen. Ray Odierno, the top U.S. military commander in Iraq, said Sunday that he believes U.S. troops will be out of the country by the end of 2011.

Odierno said the United States is working with Iraq to preserve security gains as it prepares to withdraw.

On CNN’s “State of the Union,” chief national correspondent John King asked Odierno to rate, on a scale of 1 to 10, his confidence that U.S. troops would be out of Iraq by the end of the timeline agreed upon by the U.S. and Iraqi governments.

“As you ask me today, I believe it’s a 10 — that we will be gone by 2011,” Odierno responded.

One of the key architects of the troop “surge” strategy in Iraq, Odierno said conditions in the war-torn country have “improved significantly” over the past year or so.

“Obviously, we still have some very serious incidents ... but, again, it’s much safer,” he said.

Nine U.S. troops were killed in March, the lowest monthly toll since the beginning of the Iraq War in 2003, he said.

“So, there’s been a clear improvement of security here,” Odierno said. “The issue is: Can we maintain that? Can the Iraqis maintain it? And that’s what we’re working through now. We want them to be able to maintain this stability as we pull out.”

But less than two weeks into April, the U.S. death toll for the month had already reached nine.

Asked whether the attacks were a sign of increased coordinated violence, Odierno said that “there are some cells out there who are still capable of conducting suicide attacks,” though he described those cells as “very small.”

The U.S. military has made it more difficult for foreign fighters to enter Iraq through Syria, but support for the Iraqi insurgency is still coming from Iran, he said.

Mowaffak al-Rubaie, Iraq’s national security adviser, said the Iraqi government is making progress in managing its own security.

“We, the government of Iraq and the security forces in Iraq, are much more suited now for this fight,” al-Rubaie told “State of the Union.”

“And we believe that now we are leading and we are planning and carrying out most of the combat operations in the country,” he said, “and the United States forces are moving or transitioning to a more support role — more training, more logistical support — rather than engaging in a huge military or kinetic combat operations.”

Al-Rubaie declined to comment when asked how President Obama’s approach has differed from that of former President George W. Bush.

“I don’t want to elaborate on differences,” al-Rubaie said. “But I believe that President Obama understands the situation in Iraq, and I believe he wants to stick by ... the withdrawal agreement.”

Odierno described Obama as “very attentive.”

“He listens. He’s incredibly intelligent. He talks through the issues,” Odierno said. “He makes a decision and then we execute those decisions, and that’s all you can expect out of your commander in chief. And I’ve been very pleased with the interaction that I’ve been able to have with him.”

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Gen. Ray Odierno, the senior U.S. military officer in Iraq, said Sunday that he expects American forces to leave Iraq by the close of 2011.

Odierno said the United States is coordinating with Iraq to preserve the security gains made in the country while preparing for withdrawal.

During an appearance on CNN’s “State of the Union,” chief national correspondent John King asked Odierno how confident he was, from 1 to 10, that U.S. forces would depart by the deadline established in the agreement between Washington and Baghdad.

“If you’re asking me today, I’d say it’s a 10 — that we’ll be out by 2011,” Odierno replied.

Odierno, who was one of the main planners behind the Iraq troop “surge,” said the situation in the conflict-stricken country had become “significantly” better over roughly the previous year.

“Clearly, we continue to see some very serious incidents ... but it is much safer,” he said.

He noted that nine U.S. service members were killed in March, making it the lowest monthly death toll for American troops since the Iraq War began in 2003.

“So there has been an obvious improvement in security here,” Odierno said. “The question is whether that can be sustained. Can the Iraqis sustain it? That is what we are working on now. As we withdraw, we want them to be able to preserve this stability.”

However, with April not yet two weeks old, nine U.S. troops had already been killed that month.

When asked whether the attacks suggested a rise in organized violence, Odierno said that “there are some cells out there who are still capable of conducting suicide attacks,” though he characterized those groups as “very small.”

He also said the U.S. military had made it harder for foreign fighters to enter Iraq through Syria, but added that Iran continued to provide backing for the Iraqi insurgency.

Mowaffak al-Rubaie, Iraq’s national security adviser, said Iraq’s government was improving its ability to manage security on its own.

“We, the government of Iraq and the security forces in Iraq, are much better prepared now for this fight,” al-Rubaie said on “State of the Union.”

He added that Iraqi forces now believe they are directing, organizing and carrying out most combat missions in the country, while U.S. forces are shifting into a supporting role — focusing more on training and logistics rather than taking part in large-scale military or kinetic combat operations.

Asked to compare President Obama’s approach with that of former President George W. Bush, al-Rubaie declined to go into detail.

“I don’t want to elaborate on differences,” he said. “But I believe that President Obama understands the situation in Iraq, and I believe he wants to stick by ... the withdrawal agreement.”

Odierno described Obama as “very attentive.”

“He listens. He’s extremely intelligent. He works through the issues,” Odierno said. “He reaches a decision, and then we carry out those decisions. That is what you expect from your commander-in-chief. I’ve been very pleased with the interaction I’ve had with him.”

**Odierno: U.S. troops on track to leave Iraq by end of 2011**

Gen. Ray Odierno said Sunday he is “fully confident” that U.S. troops will leave Iraq by the end of 2011, citing improved security conditions and the growing capability of Iraqi security forces.

Speaking on CNN’s “State of the Union,” the top U.S. commander in Iraq said the withdrawal timeline remains consistent with the security agreement between Washington and Baghdad, which calls for all American forces to depart Iraq by December 31, 2011.

“I feel very confident that we’ll be able to meet that timeline,” Odierno said, pointing to a sharp decline in violence from the height of the war and the increasing ability of Iraqi forces to conduct operations on their own.

Odierno said Iraqi army and police units have made significant progress in taking responsibility for security across the country. While challenges remain — including insurgent attacks and political tensions — he said Iraqi forces are increasingly capable of handling threats with limited U.S. support.

The general also said President Barack Obama’s plan to draw down U.S. forces is proceeding responsibly. Obama has pledged to end the U.S. combat mission in Iraq while maintaining a temporary advisory and training role before the full withdrawal deadline.

Odierno’s comments came as Iraqi officials continued to debate the country’s long-term security needs. Mowaffak al-Rubaie, Iraq’s former national security adviser, has said the agreement requiring U.S. troops to leave by the end of 2011 should be honored, while also acknowledging that Iraq must continue strengthening its own military and police capabilities.

The U.S. military presence in Iraq has steadily decreased as Iraqi forces have taken the lead in security operations. Odierno said the gains are real but fragile, emphasizing that continued political progress in Iraq will be critical to preserving stability after U.S. troops depart.

# Odierno: U.S. troop drawdown in Iraq on track, but security challenges remain

**BAGHDAD, Iraq —** The top U.S. commander in Iraq said the planned withdrawal of American combat forces remains on schedule, even as he warned that Iraq’s fragile security gains could still be tested by political tensions, insurgent attacks and the ability of Iraqi forces to operate independently.

Gen. Ray Odierno, commander of U.S. forces in Iraq, said in an interview that American troops are preparing to leave Iraqi cities by the end of June, in keeping with a security agreement signed by Washington and Baghdad. Under the broader timeline, U.S. combat forces are expected to leave Iraq by the end of August 2010, with all remaining American troops scheduled to depart by the end of 2011.

“We are on track,” Odierno said, while emphasizing that the transition will depend heavily on continued progress by Iraqi security forces and political leaders. “The Iraqis are increasingly taking the lead. Our job now is to support them as they build the capability to sustain security on their own.”

The comments come at a pivotal moment in the six-year-old war, as the United States shifts from a large combat presence to an advisory and support role. President Barack Obama has pledged to end the U.S. combat mission in Iraq while maintaining a residual force to train Iraqi troops, conduct limited counterterrorism operations and protect American personnel.

## Iraqi forces taking the lead

Odierno said Iraqi army and police units have improved significantly since the height of the violence in 2006 and 2007, when sectarian killings pushed the country toward civil war. He credited a combination of the U.S. troop surge, the rise of local Sunni “Awakening” groups against al Qaeda in Iraq, and the growing capacity of Iraqi security forces with reducing violence across much of the country.

But he said the next stage will be more complicated than simply reducing troop numbers.

“This is about more than withdrawal,” Odierno said. “It’s about making sure the Iraqis can handle the threats that remain.”

Those threats, he said, include al Qaeda in Iraq, extremist militias and unresolved disputes between Iraq’s ethnic and sectarian communities. While large-scale sectarian violence has declined sharply, bombings and targeted attacks continue, particularly in Baghdad, Mosul and areas of northern Iraq where Arab-Kurdish tensions remain high.

Odierno described al Qaeda in Iraq as weakened but still dangerous.

“They no longer have the freedom of movement they once had,” he said. “But they can still carry out high-profile attacks designed to undermine confidence in the government.”

## June deadline approaches

Under the U.S.-Iraq security agreement, American combat forces are to withdraw from Iraqi cities, towns and villages by June 30. Iraqi authorities have portrayed the date as a milestone in the restoration of national sovereignty.

U.S. commanders have said many American troops will move to bases outside urban areas, where they can still assist Iraqi forces if requested. Odierno said U.S. forces will remain ready to provide intelligence, logistics, air support and training, but he stressed that Iraqi commanders will increasingly make the key decisions.

“The Iraqis are in charge,” he said. “We will not operate unilaterally in the same way we did in the past.”

Still, some U.S. military officials have privately expressed concern that Iraqi units vary widely in professionalism and capability. While some army divisions are considered reliable, police forces in certain areas remain vulnerable to corruption, political influence and infiltration by militant groups.

Odierno acknowledged those concerns but said the overall trend is positive.

“There are areas where they are very good, and areas where they still need help,” he said. “That is why our advisory role is important.”

## Political tensions remain a risk

Beyond battlefield concerns, Odierno said Iraq’s long-term stability will depend on political progress. Key disputes remain unresolved, including the status of the oil-rich city of Kirkuk, the balance of power between Baghdad and the Kurdish regional government, and the integration of Sunni fighters who helped turn against al Qaeda.

The Sons of Iraq, largely Sunni security volunteers formerly backed by the U.S. military, have been a particular source of concern. Many members expected jobs in Iraq’s security forces or government ministries, but the process has moved slowly. U.S. officials have warned that failure to integrate them could fuel renewed unrest.

Odierno said the Iraqi government must continue efforts to bring those groups into the political and security structure.

“They took a stand against al Qaeda,” he said. “It is important that they see a future in the new Iraq.”

National elections, expected in 2010, are also viewed as a major test. Odierno said political competition is healthy but warned that extremists may attempt to exploit campaign tensions.

“Elections are always a period of vulnerability,” he said. “The key is that disputes are handled through the political process, not through violence.”

## U.S. mission changing

At the height of the surge, the United States had more than 160,000 troops in Iraq. That number has already fallen, and the drawdown is expected to accelerate as commanders reposition forces and close or transfer bases to Iraqi control.

Odierno said the reduction must be carried out carefully to avoid creating security gaps.

“We have a plan, and we are executing it deliberately,” he said. “The worst thing we could do is rush in a way that puts the gains at risk.”

The general said U.S. forces will continue to train Iraqi units in areas such as intelligence gathering, logistics, border security and air defense — capabilities Iraq is still developing. He noted that Iraq’s security forces have become more confident but still depend on American support for certain advanced operations.

Military analysts say that distinction will shape the U.S. role over the next two years: fewer combat patrols, more mentoring and specialized assistance.

## Violence down, uncertainty ahead

U.S. officials point to a dramatic decline in violence since the worst years of the war. Markets have reopened in Baghdad, checkpoints have been reduced in some neighborhoods, and many displaced families have begun returning home.

But the improvement remains uneven. Car bombs and suicide attacks still strike civilian targets, and the northern city of Mosul remains one of the most dangerous areas in the country. Insurgent groups continue to target Iraqi police, government officials and religious pilgrims.

Odierno said such attacks are intended to create the impression that the Iraqi government cannot protect its citizens.

“They want to shake people’s confidence,” he said. “Our assessment is that they do not have the capability to bring Iraq back to the levels of violence we saw before, but they can still cause suffering and instability.”

The commander said the coming months will reveal whether Iraqi forces can maintain momentum as U.S. troops move farther into the background.

“This is an important period,” Odierno said. “We have made real progress, but progress has to be sustained.”

For the Obama administration, the Iraq drawdown is also tied to broader military priorities, including the expanding war in Afghanistan. As U.S. commanders prepare to shift resources, Odierno said the mission in Iraq must end responsibly.

“Our goal is to leave behind an Iraq that can secure itself and govern itself,” he said. “That has always been the objective. We are closer to that today, but there is still work to do.”

Gen. Ray Odierno, the top U.S. commander in Iraq, said Sunday he is fully confident American forces will leave Iraq on schedule under the security agreement between Washington and Baghdad.

Asked on CNN’s *State of the Union* to rate his confidence — on a scale of one to 10 — that U.S. troops will be out of Iraq by the end of 2011, Odierno answered: “Ten.”

“We’re on track,” Odierno said, pointing to the continued transfer of security responsibilities to Iraqi forces and the planned drawdown of U.S. combat troops. He said commanders are watching conditions on the ground, but emphasized that the timetable remains in place.

Odierno said violence in Iraq is significantly lower than at the height of the war, though he cautioned that extremist groups still retain the ability to carry out attacks.

counterfactuals.output:
**Washington (CNN) —** The top U.S. commander in Iraq expressed confidence Tuesday that American forces can continue their planned withdrawal despite a recent spike in deadly attacks, saying Iraqi security forces are increasingly capable of protecting the country as the U.S. military shifts into a smaller, supporting role.

Gen. Ray Odierno, the commander of U.S. forces in Iraq, said the overall security trend remains positive even though April saw a series of high-profile bombings that raised concerns about whether insurgent groups were trying to exploit the drawdown of American troops.

“We have always expected that there would be attempts to test the Iraqi security forces,” Odierno said, stressing that militant networks remain dangerous but weakened. “The important thing is that the Iraqis are responding, and they are taking the lead.”

The comments came as the Obama administration moves ahead with plans to end the U.S. combat mission in Iraq and reduce the American military presence after more than six years of war. President Barack Obama has said U.S. combat forces will leave Iraq by the end of August 2010, with a smaller force remaining temporarily to train, advise and assist Iraqi troops before a full withdrawal under the U.S.-Iraq security agreement.

Odierno’s remarks reflected the delicate balance facing Washington: acknowledging the continuing threat from insurgents while maintaining confidence in the ability of Iraq’s government and security forces to assume responsibility for the country’s stability.

April attacks, including coordinated bombings in Baghdad and other cities, killed scores of Iraqis and underscored the ability of extremists to strike crowded civilian areas. U.S. officials have said the violence appears intended to undermine public confidence in the Iraqi government and provoke sectarian tensions.

But Odierno said the attacks did not represent a return to the widespread violence that gripped Iraq in earlier years. He argued that Iraqi police and army units have improved significantly in intelligence gathering, checkpoint operations and rapid response, though he acknowledged that gaps remain.

“We still have work to do,” he said. “But the Iraqi security forces are much better than they were even a year ago.”

Under the evolving mission, U.S. troops are increasingly stepping back from direct combat operations and moving into advisory and support roles. American units are working with Iraqi forces on logistics, intelligence, planning and training, while Iraqi commanders take greater control of day-to-day security operations.

That transition is a central part of Obama’s Iraq policy. The president has sought to wind down the war while shifting attention and resources toward Afghanistan and other national security priorities. At the same time, administration officials have emphasized that the withdrawal must be responsible and conditions-based enough to avoid jeopardizing fragile security gains.

Military officials say the drawdown will require careful coordination, not only in reducing troop numbers but also in moving large amounts of equipment out of the country and closing or transferring bases to Iraqi control.

Odierno said he remains optimistic that the plan can be carried out on schedule. He said the United States will continue to monitor the security environment closely, but he suggested that recent attacks have not changed the broader assessment that Iraqi forces are prepared to take on more responsibility.

The coming months will be a major test for Iraq’s security institutions. As U.S. troops leave cities and reduce their combat footprint, Iraqi forces will be judged on their ability to prevent large-scale violence, protect civilians and maintain public confidence.

For the Obama administration, the withdrawal is both a strategic goal and a political promise. For Odierno and commanders on the ground, it is a complex military operation that depends heavily on whether Iraqi forces can hold the security gains achieved after years of war.

“We are moving from being in the lead to enabling the Iraqis,” Odierno said. “That is the future of our mission.”
